title: Trend Following over the next few years - Systematic Investor 314

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Trend Following over the next few years - Systematic Investor 314.docx

speakers: Mark Rzepczynski (host/guest, systematic researcher; caption 'Mark rinsky')
summary: Mark and Niels discuss September 2024 trend-following results, the Fed 50bp cut, post-event behaviour and the KUU framework. Topics: algo aversion, explaining models, market connectedness, adaptive markets, bear-market memory and CTA index replication. Main idea: systematic managers respond to prices after events and stay diversified instead of forecasting.

coverage.note: Waymo aside; trend update, index numbers, macro trends
carry unwind, trend-carry blend, carry size, Fed and carry
Fed 50bp cut, uncertainty, bond reaction, post-event behaviour
post-event approach, three-way separation, Jackson Hole commentary (no extra claim)
central bank skin in game, cut at all-time highs
blame on systems vs humans, trust in models
bear market memory, turning points, passive flows
replicator manager risk, median vs benchmark; outro

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - the first reader caught the main frameworks (post-event behaviour, KUU, connectedness, adaptive markets, replicators); missed secondary ideas on Jackson Hole and central bank narratives, passive vs active under KUU, discretionary vs systematic investor bar, spillover decomposition and the 20% correction point.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we've had replication for a lot of hedge fund strategies including manage Futures and now people are saying it's like can we do this for private equity
claims.claim: Replication, already done for hedge fund strategies including managed futures, is being attempted for private equity indices to create a liquid version of an illiquid asset, which raises many quant and replication problems.
claims.testable: partly - replication tracking error can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Financial Engineers will come in and take something that is definitely IL liquid and by way of matching making it liquid which of course it it isn't
claims.claim: Financial engineering can create the perception of liquidity for inherently illiquid assets, which is a risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: most of the performance is coming from sectors like fixed income precious metals
claims.claim: In mid/late Sept 2024 trend-follower gains came from fixed income and precious metals, with sugar and grain counter-trend rallies hurting and coffee strength helping.
claims.indicator: sector P&L: fixed income, precious metals, sugar, grains, coffee
claims.direction: long coffee, long bonds and precious metals profitable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own Trend barometer yesterday finished at 45 so that's pretty neutral
claims.claim: Niels' trend barometer was 45 (neutral) on 25 Sep 2024; reported index numbers: BTOP50 +1.18% September (+3.92% YTD), SG CTA +1% (+2.42%), SG Trend +1.42% (+2.72%), short-term traders +0.82%, MSCI World +0.77% (+16.42%), S&P 500 +1.16% (~+20%).
claims.indicator: Top Traders trend barometer, BTOP50, SG indices

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: macro Trends macro Trends macro trends that the macro environment
claims.claim: Macro trends (growth path and interest-rate direction) will drive price trends and hence trend-following performance through the rest of 2024 and early 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: reversals uh led to the uh carry uh onwi
claims.claim: The August 2024 carry unwind (yen reversal) hurt trend followers to some extent.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: because they're uncorrelated how do you blend the two of those together to come up with a better strategy
claims.claim: Trend and carry are uncorrelated and can be blended; carry does well in risk-on, trend does well in risk-off, which drives their low or negative correlation.
claims.direction: carry long in risk-on, trend long in risk-off
claims.testable: yes - blend backtest conditional on risk regime

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: there's a tremendous amount of uncertainty surrounding carry because we never really know how large it is
claims.claim: The size of carry as a strategy class is highly uncertain (estimates range from hundreds of billions to trillions) and 'carry' means different things (short-term active carry vs long-term mega carry across countries).
claims.testable: partly - data on positioning is limited

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: most investors prefer nothing happens really or nothing happening and at the same time they can earn a little bit of money every day
claims.claim: Investors prefer carry-like payoffs that earn a little each day when nothing happens, making it hard to sell trend following which pays when markets move.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker. The passage begins 'indeed and actually you could say...' and ends 'but what you said about carry also nicely feeds into our first topic', so it is Niels replying to Mark, not Mark.
correction.fix: Niels (replying to Mark) says carry runs through society as a whole and ties to trend following because most investors prefer nothing to happen while earning a little every day, which is the challenge trend followers face in selling a strategy that pays when markets move.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the fed and other central banks have really been responsible for the rise of the carry regime
claims.claim: Central bank policies over decades fostered the carry regime (forward guidance reducing uncertainty).
claims.indicator: central bank forward guidance and carry

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the day before the the Wednesday announcement it was almost a a 5050 chance between there being a 50 basis point and a 25 basis point C
claims.claim: The Fed's 50bp cut in Sept 2024 came with maximum market uncertainty (50/50 pricing the day before, versus usual 90-95% certainty), contradicting its forward guidance aim; a 50bp move usually signals a major policy reversal.
claims.indicator: fed funds futures pricing before FOMC

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you look at the 10year and 30-year uh bond prices they actually fell
claims.claim: After the 50bp cut the dollar did not set a new low and 10- and 30-year Treasury prices fell, the opposite of the usual response, suggesting long-end investors did not want to hold bonds.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the GDP now forecast which is from the Atlanta Fed
claims.claim: Atlanta Fed GDPNow was around 3% for the next quarter, well above Blue Chip consensus, so the Fed's 50bp cut looked odd given strong growth, above-target inflation and no recession precipice.
claims.indicator: Atlanta Fed GDPNow vs Blue Chip

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they're always interested in what we call postevent Behavior we don't care about what the FED may do as a forecast
claims.claim: Systematic managers care about post-event behaviour (what happens after an action) rather than forecasting the event, so past 50bp cut episodes could be studied but the sample is small.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: I'll take advantage of that adjustment period post event
claims.claim: A trend follower does not forecast the Fed but follows portfolio adjustments after the event, and diversification across dollar, oil, equities and fixed income lets him exploit secondary effects across markets.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what is the market going to tell me in prices and how do I then exploit that
claims.claim: Separate three things: what I think they should do, how the market perceives it, and what the market's price reaction says; the third drives the trade (continuation, reversal or mean reversion).

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the central Bankers often don't have skin in the game
claims.claim: Central bankers lack skin in the game, unlike traders who lose clients and assets when they underperform.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: how many times has a central bank caught by 50 basis points at the same time as the equity markets being at new all-time highs
claims.claim: A 50bp cut with equities at all-time highs is nearly unprecedented, and with low volatility and low uncertainty the cut looks rash; markets were not signalling a problem.
claims.indicator: Fed cut vs equity all-time highs

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what is known what is unknown and then what is unknowable
claims.claim: The KUU (known, unknown, unknowable) framework: act on what is measurable, avoid what cannot be handicapped, and diversify against the unknowable.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: right around that election date you're going to see heightened volatility because that's when uncertainty is going to be resolved
claims.claim: Volatility rises around known-date events like the US election because uncertainty resolves then; the outcome is unknown but not unknowable.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the revisions and unemployment that we saw was something that was unknowable
claims.claim: The one-million-job downward employment revision was unknowable, so the response is to follow prices.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the one thing that kind of helps on all fronts with this is just being Diversified
claims.claim: True diversification (about 100 markets in a trend portfolio rather than 100 stocks) helps against the unknown and unknowable.
claims.indicator: number of markets in trend portfolio
claims.testable: yes - diversification benefit vs number of markets

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the correlation between stocks and bonds is positive well then if you're long then that's not going to Long only that's not going to help you
claims.claim: Long-only is not enough when stock-bond correlation is positive; trend followers who go long and short across asset classes handle the unknown best.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: investors were a little bit slower at responding to that new bit of information than if it was generated by a human
claims.claim: Studies show algo aversion: investors respond slower to information generated by AI/algorithms than to the same information from humans, even if algorithms forecast better.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's being blamed right but then when I think about this being a human
claims.claim: Systematic funds are blamed for losses (the system's fault) whereas discretionary managers' losses are excused as unforeseeable.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: as humans we're willing to forgive other humans we're unforgiving with respect to system and and models
claims.claim: People forgive human managers (who give excuses) but not models, which cannot make excuses, so they do not trust models.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: following the models in generally would be better off than actually turning the model off or reversing what the model told you to do
claims.claim: Following the model is usually better than overriding it in a one-off situation, though a mechanism for override exists.
claims.testable: yes - compare override vs no override

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there were quite a few managers who um stepped in
claims.claim: Several managers overrode models in March 2020 for risk management; a backtest is worth little if you tinker with the model.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the number one flaw with systematic and Trend f following managers in general is that managers are not very good about explaining what they do
claims.claim: Systematic managers explain what they do poorly, and investors ask poor questions; the key is stating when and why a model should do well or poorly, not the tautology 'when there are trends'.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we will go with a market move or a trend for as long as it will take us even if it's never taken even even if it's never done this before
claims.claim: A rules-based approach avoids anchoring: it follows moves even if unprecedented, e.g. 10-year yields falling below 2% and to negative rates when many believed they could not.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: are you using a 20-day or a 30-day uh volatility flaw for example
claims.claim: Detailed parameter questions (20 vs 30 day volatility lookback) do not help investors understand future performance.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: there's a difference between performance attribution and contribution
claims.claim: Attribution (why money was made in crude or bonds, and which conditions allowed it) is more informative than contribution (how much was made per market).

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what is market connectedness what are the correlations and what's the potential for contagion
claims.claim: Three C's: connectedness, correlation and contagion; treat markets as a network of nodes whose connectedness (clusters, common traders, similar events) drives dynamic correlations.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the behavior of one market will spill over to another and that's an opportunity for exploitation
claims.claim: Portfolio construction should also exploit market connectedness: a Fed move spills to equities, bonds, dollar, then oil and commodities after a short delay, so cross-correlations and cross-trends could be used.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: as soon as you go outside uh the the the sector itself I think there are relatively few sectors where you can have high confidence in any kind of reaction pattern
claims.claim: Reaction patterns are reliable only within a sector (e.g. financials); beyond that few have high confidence, and trend following's strength is not needing to know how things play out.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we do know that markets trade in clusters so we know that there's a base metal clustered
claims.claim: Markets trade in clusters (base metals driven by business cycle, precious metals, energy) with spillovers to the real economy.
claims.indicator: base metals, precious metals, energy clusters

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if you're a trend follower you really believe in an Adaptive markets hypothesis
claims.claim: Efficiency is dynamic (Andy Lo's adaptive markets hypothesis): varies by liquidity, valuation difficulty, hedger/speculator mix, participants and cycle, so trends can exist; markets are efficient but not all the time.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: social media is driving uh markets to be less efficient and that there's more gamesmanship
claims.claim: Cliff Asness argues social media makes markets less efficient; Mark takes a more nuanced dynamic view.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you could be 40 years old and never seen a a a large bare market
claims.claim: Many market participants (including central bankers) have never experienced a large bear market, so their collective memory is poor and they expect policy to always support markets.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the systematic manager should be able to have a plan in place because his models allows for going both long and short
claims.claim: Systematic managers backtest over long history, so a plan exists for equity declines (sell/short) even if the manager has not lived through a bear market.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is a pickup of volatility around these big turning points um and that in itself actually often triggers Trend followers to reduce their risk
claims.claim: Volatility picks up around trend turning points which makes trend followers cut risk, though sharp reversals still hurt.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: flows from passive Investments and and what that's going to do once the markets
claims.claim: Passive flows could amplify a sustained market decline, unlike the short 2-3 week dips since the central bank rescues of recent years.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they look at uh what is the top uh managers in terms of AUM and then they adjust this once a year
claims.claim: The SG index is built from the largest managers by AUM, reconstituted yearly; a diversified portfolio of selected CTAs should be able to beat it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's giant back test of a model uh people should be aware of that
claims.claim: The new SG investable CTA index is a giant backtest of a model, and buying a CTA replicator index is not the same as buying a stock index.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think there's a huge manager risk and often these replicators run very small firms much smaller than the underlying managers
claims.claim: Replicators carry manager risk too: they are small firms whose models could be flawed.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: a median uh replication strategy is not a benchmark replication
claims.claim: Replicators aim for median manager returns, not a benchmark; median replication is suitable for low-cost investors with no manager skill, while most managers underperform their benchmarks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: our systems will automatically take this into account because they're sampling uh you know a new data set that includes the day I the price move
claims.claim: Trend systems react to an event only through the new price data: the post-event move enters the sample at once, but it takes time to change the signal, so adaptation lags the event.
claims.direction: trend positions adjust after the price move, not before
claims.testable: yes - measure signal response time after policy-event price moves

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we know whatever happened this week was probably in the cards uh even when Jackson Hall um was being held in in August
claims.claim: The September 2024 Fed cut was foreshadowed at the August Jackson Hole speeches (Powell: price stability under control, focus turning to the employment leg of the dual mandate), so the policy pivot itself was telegraphed even though the size (25 vs 50bp) was not.
claims.testable: partly - compare Jackson Hole signals with subsequent policy moves

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: extreme policies like Zer QE fate um which were explic itly targeted at generating inflation are never attributed as having a role in the subsequent inflation
claims.claim: Reading David Dredge: central banks never attribute the later inflation to their own extreme policies (zero rates, QE aimed at generating inflation), credit their latest tightening for restoring price stability, and blame exogenous shocks (Bailey cited Covid/Ukraine about 50 times), so their narratives are self-serving and a weak guide to future policy.
claims.indicator: central bank communication and inflation attribution

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if you fall into the camp that there's a lot more unknowable information and there's a lot more Unknown about the world then you probably want to be more of a passive investor
claims.claim: Under the KUU framework, the more of the world one judges to be unknown or unknowable (and managers unable to know more than the market), the more sensible passive indexing is; Niels counters that the real lesson is true diversification (about 100 markets), which works for both active and passive.
claims.conditions: depends on belief about how much is knowable

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: that still requires a lot of fundamental research to be able to say what are exogenous factors
claims.claim: Explaining when trend following works needs fundamental research into exogenous, non-price conditions (macro and environmental factors necessary or sufficient for positive trend returns), which is an open research agenda beyond the tautology 'it does well when there are trends'.
claims.testable: yes - regress trend returns on macro and environment variables

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the advantage of a discretionary trade of course is that they can anticipate which a model can't do and and if they're very good at that that has value of course
claims.claim: A discretionary trader can anticipate (e.g. regime breaks) where a rules-based model cannot, which has value if done well, so a combination of systematic and discretionary approaches might be better than either alone.
claims.conditions: only if the discretionary manager is genuinely skilled

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the bar that's set by investors is much higher for systematic managers than a discretionary manager
claims.claim: Investors demand far more detail of systematic managers (lookback, testing, process) than they ever ask of discretionary managers whose decision process is no more transparent, so systematic managers must explain the 'why' not just the parameters.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: your Trend speed should be 3 months that's the best right well based on what evidence uh would you say that or you have to trade 500 markets that must be better than trading 100 markets
claims.claim: Investors often hold untested beliefs about system design (the best trend speed is three months; trading 500 markets must beat 100) that clash with a manager's evidence, so claims about speed and market count need evidence, not assertion.
claims.indicator: trend speed; number of markets traded (100 vs 500)
claims.testable: yes - compare Sharpe by trend speed and by market-universe size

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we should be able to decompose a shock and stocks on what it will on the impact on other markets and if we can know the direction of causality from one set of markets to another
claims.claim: Variance (shock) decomposition of cross-market spillovers could reveal the direction of causality between markets (a stock shock feeding bonds, dollar, commodities), which would guide portfolio construction, risk and opportunities.
claims.indicator: variance decomposition / directional spillover measures across markets
claims.conditions: Niels doubts spillover patterns are reliable outside a single sector
claims.testable: yes - estimate directional spillover indices and test lead-lag trades

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: a 20% correction in the stock market which would be a bare Market uh is you have a Devastation on a lot of people's wealth but on many measures that wouldn't really sort of eliminate all the overvaluation in stocks
claims.claim: A 20% equity bear market would only take back about a year and a half of returns and not remove the overvaluation, yet policymakers (calls for a 75bp cut after the August 2024 carry unwind) act to prevent it; this shows over-sensitivity of policy to modest equity declines.
claims.direction: policy support for equities (Fed put) expected on small declines
claims.conditions: recent memory of only short dips, quickly rescued
claims.testable: partly - compare policy reaction thresholds with drawdown depth

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: he's also basically suggesting that investors should try and find managers who strive to be different from the index and ideally of course be better uh than the index
claims.claim: Citing Transtrend and Michael Green's 'Why bother being better': investors should look for managers who strive to differ from and beat the index rather than simply buying the CTA index, since passive concentration distorts markets and an index is not risk-free.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index versus selected managers
claims.testable: partly - manager-selection value added versus the index
